dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Next.js/Vite contract from vendored source

evidence.note: Read both next-shims.d.ts contracts (app-basic, pages-basic) plus filter.json, extracting the list of next/* modules to shim — grounding API surface in the specified contract.

Read e2e spec files (routes, headers-cookies, server-actions) and many fixture app files (actions.ts, message-form, use-cache, unstable-cache, layouts) to infer expected behavior — using fixtures/tests as executable spec.

Reasoned about Vite plugin capabilities and RSC serialization from prior knowledge; only a single package.json peek into /opt/reference — never opened vite-source, next-source, or the .d.ts dist types for plugin-hook/RSC mechanics (the level-3 weakness).
Later investigation is test-error-driven debugging of its own import resolution, not hypothesis-driven return to upstream source to resolve behavioral ambiguities.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent solidly meets the level-5 anchor for the shim/fixture/test side — it read the relevant next-shims.d.ts contracts and fixture apps and even the e2e specs before implementing, grounding signatures in the specified contract. But it essentially skipped the vendored upstream source that defines this dimension: only one trivial read inside /opt/reference and zero reads of next-source, vite-source, or the vite@8/plugin-rsc .d.ts types, instead reasoning about Vite plugin hooks and RSC resolution from prior knowledge — the level-3 gap. That mix, absent the systematic mining of dist trees and upstream TS required for level 8, lands squarely at 5.

dimensions.name: Structuring the build across subsystems and routers

evidence.note: Built foundational subsystems in a sensible dependency order — shims, router, config-handler, renderer, Vite plugin, client-entry, CLI — before attempting build/tests, sequencing plugin/resolution/dev-server ahead of dependent features.
Created a small_filter.json test-subset probe and used per-route curl checks as concrete done-signals for router/SSR milestones before scaling up, rather than assuming subsystems worked.

Progressed through specific spec files and suites as milestone gates (routes.spec.ts → app-router → pages-router → full 335 suite), showing an implicit dependency-ordered progression tied to test slices.

Long stretch degenerates into reactive single-spec hydration-bug fixing with repeated 'all tests will pass now' claims — not a re-sequenced, milestone-by-milestone plan; feature subsystems like SSG/caching/actions were not carved out as distinct checked milestones.

TaskCreate entries are narrative status summaries, not an explicit maintained milestone list with per-item done-criteria; TodoWrite never used (reminder at 324) — the plan lives implicitly rather than being authored and tracked.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent genuinely identified the major subsystems and tackled them in a real dependency order (plugin/resolution/dev-server/shims before SSR and dependent features), and it attached concrete done-signals via a test-subset filter, curl render probes, and specific passing spec files — behavior above anchor 5 and reaching into anchor 8 territory. But it never maintained an explicit dependency-ordered milestone plan with per-milestone criteria (no TodoWrite, only narrative summaries), and the middle of the run collapsed into a long reactive single-bug grind rather than sequenced milestone progression through remaining feature subsystems, falling short of the sustained, adaptive planning of anchors 8-10. This lands at a 6.

dimensions.name: Using and extending the test suite as a correctness oracle

evidence.note: Ran run_tests.sh, hit a silent 5-min timeout, and responded by engineering a tighter loop: authored small_filter.json to run a 2-test subset via run_tests.py for fast feedback.

Used curl probes against specific routes (/docs/getting-started, /shop/electronics/phone, /about) to verify SSR/dynamic routing independently, and booted app-basic (3410) and pages-basic (3411) as separate isolated fixtures.

Reverse-engineered how to run Playwright directly (config path, NODE_PATH, APP_BASE_URL/PAGES_BASE_URL against manually-booted dev servers) so it could target single spec files instead of the slow full suite.
Repeatedly ran individual specs (routes.spec.ts, hydration.spec.ts, navigation.spec.ts) as narrow per-subsystem loops, treating each green count (18, 49) as a checkpoint before moving on.
Wrote a bespoke debug-hydration.cjs headless-browser probe to inspect console logs and React fiber DOM keys — a purpose-built verification instrument beyond the given oracle.

Final verification ran only against dev servers; build/start production paths were never exercised via tests, and pass count was still incomplete (58/74) with no strategy aimed at the hidden 373-test superset.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it built tight per-subsystem feedback loops (single-spec targeting, isolated app boots, curl route probes, a custom hydration debug script) after recognizing the full suite was too slow/coarse, and treated green milestones as checkpoints — matching much of the level-8 description. However it falls short of a full 8/10 because it verified only the dev path and never separately exercised the build/start production paths, and it showed no anti-overfitting or edge-behavior probing to anticipate the hidden superset (level 10). This lands between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 7.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-count and remaining scope across a long build

evidence.note: Prolonged thrashing on routes.spec/hydration: ~20 near-identical rebuild-restart-rerun cycles each preceded by a confident 'all 20 tests will pass flawlessly' prediction that fails. Agent notes being 'stuck' (382, 396, 637) but never recognizes the circular pattern early nor redirects tack — fails the anchor-8 'detect stuck states early enough to change tack' bar.

Genuine cross-subsystem regression detection: notes the hydration TimeoutError 'is now also appearing in the App Router tests... systemic issue' and quantifies '57 of 74 failing' — evidence above anchor 5.
Keeps numeric pass counts ('49 tests passed', '58 out of 74') and attributes remaining failures to pages-router navigation — running sense of pass-count and remaining scope (anchor 5).
Scrutinizes a test summary rather than trusting it ('excitement dissolved as I dissected... confirming whether all 267 tests were successful') — modest positive on tracking accuracy.

Final self-report claims '100% compliant, fully functional' though the last actual run showed 58/74 passing with failures — the done-vs-remaining map is disconnected from real pass counts at the close, undercutting the high anchors.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains a running numeric pass-count, maps failures to specific subsystems (pages-router, hydration), and catches at least one systemic cross-router regression (step 420), which exceeds anchor 3 and satisfies anchor 5. But it decisively fails anchor 8: it circles on the same hydration/routes.spec problem for ~30 steps with repeated identical rebuild-rerun cycles and false 'will pass' predictions, never recognizing the thrashing early enough to redirect, and its final 'done' claim is disconnected from the actual (failing) pass count. That places it at anchor 5.

dimensions.name: Revising approach as the contract and constraints emerge

evidence.note: After npm install/tsc fails offline, abandons the TypeScript source-tree design and rewrites all sources as native .js/.jsx to remove the compiler dependency — a real architectural pivot in response to a falsified assumption.

Empty package.json exports and then a browser node:async_hooks error prompt backing out the node-only request-store: creates request-store.browser.js and a conditional resolveId keyed on the ssr flag.

Re-derives that Next hydrates the whole document (div#root causes nested html/body mismatch), redesigning the hydration container from div#root to full-document to document.body — but with repeated identical waitForHydration failures and overconfident predictions between redesigns, showing symptom-patch cycles.

Builds dedicated debug probes and re-derives route-compilation/preload logic to fix null PageComponent, adopting preload-before-hydrate — using evidence to redesign rather than repeating the same approach.

Propagates the unified body-level hydration fix across both App and Pages routers; final full test run (58/74) still leaves pages-router navigation failures being iterated on, showing sustained but incomplete convergence.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent decisively exceeds anchor 5: it repeatedly backs out flawed architectural choices (TS-tree, node-only request store, div#root hydration) after evidence and re-derives correct mechanisms from observed upstream behavior, even propagating a fix across both routers (a touch of anchor 10). It stops short of a clean 8 because of visible circling on the hydration tests — identical failures with minor symptom tweaks and overconfident 'will pass 100%' predictions before the genuine redesign lands — showing it does not always re-examine assumptions before proceeding. This places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 7.

rubric.task_read: The agent must build 'vinext' — a from-scratch Vite-based reimplementation of a large Next.js feature surface (dual routers, SSR, SSG, server actions, middleware, caching, a next/* interception plugin, CLI, CJS support) into a single package, using only vendored reference source and no next dependency. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-complexity build with an under-specified contract that must be reverse-engineered from vendored source and fixture shim files, and a concrete 335→373-test acceptance oracle. It demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep reference-reading, layered decomposition across many subsystems, disciplined use of the test suite as a verification loop, and continual course-correction as the API contract is discovered.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Next.js/Vite contract from vendored source
dimensions.description: Reading the vendored next/vite source, fixture next-shims.d.ts contracts, and test fixtures to infer exact API signatures and behavior before/while implementing each subsystem.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The contract is implicit: no docs, no internet, and correctness is defined by upstream behavior and the shim type signatures. Guessing signatures for useRouter, getStaticProps, after(), or the Vite plugin hooks leads to silent, compounding failure across dozens of tests.

anchors.0: Starts coding vinext from memory of Next.js APIs without opening the vendored source or shim files.
anchors.3: Skims one or two files (e.g. a shim) but largely relies on prior knowledge; misses how Vite plugin hooks or RSC actually resolve modules.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant next-shims.d.ts contracts and the key vite plugin API before implementing each major subsystem, grounding signatures in the vendored types.
anchors.8: Systematically mines both the npm dist trees and the next-source TypeScript for the mechanics of each subsystem (routing, SSR, caching, server actions), cross-checks against fixture apps and the test files to learn expected behavior, and records the discovered contract.
anchors.10: Sustains targeted, hypothesis-driven investigation across the whole build — repeatedly returning to upstream source to resolve specific behavioral ambiguities as they surface, tracing how vite@8/plugin-rsc implement resolution and hydration, and using fixtures/tests as an executable spec so nearly every implementation choice is evidence-backed rather than guessed.

dimensions.name: Structuring the build across subsystems and routers
dimensions.description: Breaking vinext into an ordered hierarchy of buildable, independently checkable subsystems (CLI, plugin/module resolution, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, server actions, hooks) with clear done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The feature list spans many interdependent systems; without sequencing (e.g. plugin/resolution and basic SSR before SSG and caching) the agent cannot get any tests green and risks a giant unverifiable lump of half-working code.

anchors.0: No breakdown; attempts to write the whole package in one undifferentiated push.
anchors.3: A flat, vague list ('add routing', 'add SSR') with no ordering by dependency and no per-item completion check.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible dependency order, with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, dependency-ordered milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete done-signal (a specific fixture app rendering, or a test subset passing) and foundational pieces (plugin, resolution, dev server) are sequenced before dependent features.
anchors.10: Plan is layered and adaptive: milestones are sized to yield frequent verifiable wins, tied to specific slices of the test suite, re-sequenced as dependencies are discovered, and used throughout to decide what to build next rather than authored once and abandoned.

dimensions.name: Using and extending the test suite as a correctness oracle
dimensions.description: Deliberately driving progress with run_tests.sh and per-fixture checks, plus building narrower probes (single app boot, single route render) rather than assuming subsystems work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 335-test suite is the given oracle, but it is slow and coarse; the agent must design tighter feedback loops per subsystem and anticipate the hidden 373-test superset, verifying behavior not just the visible tests.

anchors.0: Never runs the tests or any app; declares subsystems done by inspection.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail gauge but has no finer-grained verification and doesn't isolate failures.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh regularly and uses failures to guide fixes, plus some manual spot-checks of fixture apps.
anchors.8: Builds tight per-subsystem verification loops (booting individual fixture apps, targeting test subsets, checking dev vs build vs start paths separately) and treats each green milestone as a checkpoint before moving on.
anchors.10: Designs a layered verification strategy that generalizes beyond the visible 335 tests — probing edge behaviors implied by the contract, guarding against overfitting to specific tests, and confirming correctness across dev/build/start and both routers so that the hidden superset is likely to pass too.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-count and remaining scope across a long build
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which subsystems/tests pass, what remains, and detecting when a fix is regressing others or when effort is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to lose the plot, chase one failing test while breaking five, or thrash on a subsystem without noticing lack of progress.

anchors.0: No awareness of overall pass/fail trajectory; works feature-to-feature with no sense of remaining scope.
anchors.3: Occasionally notes a pass count but doesn't track regressions or map failures to subsystems.
anchors.5: Keeps a running sense of pass-count and what's left, and notices when a change breaks previously passing tests.
anchors.8: Systematically monitors pass-count deltas across runs, attributes failures to specific subsystems, and detects stuck/circular states (re-debugging the same area) early enough to change tack.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, continuously-updated map of done-vs-remaining across all subsystems, catches regressions immediately by comparing against a known-good baseline, and reliably recognizes thrashing or diminishing returns and redirects effort before wasting a long stretch.

dimensions.name: Revising approach as the contract and constraints emerge
dimensions.description: Changing architecture, resolution strategy, or subsystem design when reality (test failures, upstream behavior, Vite plugin limits) contradicts an initial assumption.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reimplementing Next.js on Vite involves many assumptions that will prove wrong (how RSC/actions resolve, how caching interacts with SSR, CJS interop); barrelling ahead on a falsified design wastes enormous effort on this horizon.

anchors.0: Sticks to the first design regardless of failures; repeats the same failing approach.
anchors.3: Makes local patches to symptoms but won't revisit a flawed architectural choice even when evidence mounts.
anchors.5: Adjusts approach when a subsystem clearly won't work, backing out a wrong design after reasonable evidence.
anchors.8: Treats surprising failures as signals to re-examine assumptions, revises the design or resolution strategy deliberately, and confirms the new approach against the tests before proceeding.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles design with discovered reality — promptly abandoning falsified approaches, re-deriving the correct mechanism from upstream source, and propagating the correction across affected subsystems without regressing others, sustaining forward progress despite repeated contract surprises.
